claim: Postsynaptic compartments can be specifically modulated during various forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: Postsynaptic compartments can be specifically modulated during various forms of synaptic plasticity, but it is unclear whether this precision is shared at presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a general statement about synaptic plasticity that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: It is unclear whether the precision of specific modulation is shared at presynaptic terminals.
source: Postsynaptic compartments can be specifically modulated during various forms of synaptic plasticity, but it is unclear whether this precision is shared at presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) stabilizes neurotransmission at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
source: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) stabilizes neurotransmission at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, where a retrograde enhancement of presynaptic neurotransmitter release compensates for diminished postsynaptic receptor functionality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PHP at the Drosophila NMJ, supported by prior research in the field.

claim: A retrograde enhancement of presynaptic neurotransmitter release compensates for diminished postsynaptic receptor functionality during PHP.
source: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) stabilizes neurotransmission at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, where a retrograde enhancement of presynaptic neurotransmitter release compensates for diminished postsynaptic receptor functionality.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of PHP, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: PHP can be induced and expressed at a subset of synapses over both acute and chronic time scales.
source: We find that PHP can be induced and expressed at a subset of synapses, over both acute and chronic time scales, without influencing transmission at adjacent release sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PHP induction and expression at a subset of synapses does not influence transmission at adjacent release sites.
source: We find that PHP can be induced and expressed at a subset of synapses, over both acute and chronic time scales, without influencing transmission at adjacent release sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data showing no change in quantal content at muscle 7 when PHP is expressed at muscle 6.

claim: Homeostatic modulations to CaMKII are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
source: Further, homeostatic modulations to CaMKII, vesicle pools, and functional release sites are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7 showing pCaMKII reductions only at muscle 6 Ib boutons.

claim: Homeostatic modulations to vesicle pools are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
source: Further, homeostatic modulations to CaMKII, vesicle pools, and functional release sites are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
evidence: This is supported by RRP measurements in Figure 5 showing increased RRP only at muscle 6.

claim: Homeostatic modulations to functional release sites are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
source: Further, homeostatic modulations to CaMKII, vesicle pools, and functional release sites are compartmentalized and do not spread to neighboring pre- or post-synaptic structures.
evidence: This is supported by variance-mean analysis in Figure 6 showing increased N only at muscle 6.

claim: Both PHP induction and expression mechanisms are locally transmitted and restricted to specific synaptic compartments.
source: Thus, both PHP induction and expression mechanisms are locally transmitted and restricted to specific synaptic compartments.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Compartmentalized changes in dendritic spines tune responses to neurotransmitter release during information transfer in the nervous system.
source: Synaptic strength can be modulated with a remarkable degree of specificity to enable the flexibility necessary for learning and memory, where compartmentalized changes in dendritic spines tune responses to neurotransmitter release during information transfer in the nervous system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about synaptic plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Compartmentalized plasticity mechanisms require compartmentalized trafficking and insertion of glutamate receptors into postsynaptic densities at specific locations in response to correlated activity.
source: Such plasticity mechanisms require compartmentalized trafficking and insertion of glutamate receptors (GluRs) into postsynaptic densities at specific locations in response to correlated activity (Herring and Nicoll, 2016; Malinow, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hebbian plasticity processes are inherently destabilizing.
source: However, these processes of Hebbian plasticity are inherently destabilizing, and homeostatic mechanisms have been proposed to adaptively counteract such forces to maintain synaptic strength within physiologically stable levels (Davis, 2013; Pozo and Goda, 2010; Turrigiano, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Homeostatic mechanisms adaptively counteract destabilizing forces to maintain synaptic strength within physiologically stable levels.
source: However, these processes of Hebbian plasticity are inherently destabilizing, and homeostatic mechanisms have been proposed to adaptively counteract such forces to maintain synaptic strength within physiologically stable levels (Davis, 2013; Pozo and Goda, 2010; Turrigiano, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is evidence for heterogeneity in presynaptic efficacy.
source: There is evidence for heterogeneity in presynaptic efficacy (Branco et al., 2008; Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997; Holderith et al., 2012; Trommershäuser et al., 2003; Vitureira et al., 2011), and release probability can vary considerably along a single axon (Murthy et al., 1997; Paul et al., 2015; Peled and Isacoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Release probability can vary considerably along a single axon.
source: There is evidence for heterogeneity in presynaptic efficacy (Branco et al., 2008; Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997; Holderith et al., 2012; Trommershäuser et al., 2003; Vitureira et al., 2011), and release probability can vary considerably along a single axon (Murthy et al., 1997; Paul et al., 2015; Peled and Isacoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Target-specific differences in presynaptic function have been demonstrated.
source: Further, target-specific differences in presynaptic function (Frank, 1973; Katz et al., 1993; Scanziani et al., 1998) and homeostatic plasticity (Davis and Goodman, 1998) have been demonstrated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Target-specific differences in homeostatic plasticity have been demonstrated.
source: Further, target-specific differences in presynaptic function (Frank, 1973; Katz et al., 1993; Scanziani et al., 1998) and homeostatic plasticity (Davis and Goodman, 1998) have been demonstrated.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological perturbations to postsynaptic receptors initiate a retrograde, trans-synaptic signaling system that homeostatically increases presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
source: At this glutamatergic synapse, genetic and pharmacological perturbations to postsynaptic receptors initiates a retrograde, trans-synaptic signaling system that homeostatically increases presynaptic neurotransmitter release to maintain stable levels of synaptic strength (Davis and Müller, 2015; Frank, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PHP supported by citations.

claim: PHP is achieved through an increase in presynaptic efficacy.
source: This form of plasticity is achieved through an increase in presynaptic efficacy and is therefore referred to as presynaptic homeostatic potentiation (PHP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of PHP.

claim: Parallel forms of homeostatic regulation are conserved at NMJs of rodents.
source: Parallel forms of homeostatic regulation are conserved at NMJs of rodents (Wang et al., 2016b) and humans (Cull-Candy et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parallel forms of homeostatic regulation are conserved at NMJs of humans.
source: Parallel forms of homeostatic regulation are conserved at NMJs of rodents (Wang et al., 2016b) and humans (Cull-Candy et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PHP initiates a single retrograde signaling system that triggers two key expression mechanisms: increases in presynaptic calcium influx and the number of synaptic vesicles participating in the readily releasable pool.
source: PHP initiates a single retrograde signaling system that triggers two key expression mechanisms to enhance presynaptic glutamate release: increases in both presynaptic calcium influx and the number of synaptic vesicles participating in the readily releasable pool (Goel et al., 2017; Kiragasi et al., 2017; Müller and Davis, 2012; Weyhersmüller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several genes necessary for PHP expression have been identified that function as putative retrograde signals.
source: Several genes necessary for PHP expression have been identified that function as putative retrograde signals (Orr et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and presynaptic effectors in the motor neuron (Bruckner et al., 2017; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Dickman et al., 2012; Kiragasi et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012; Tsurudome et al., 2010; Younger et al., 2013), but the postsynaptic induction mechanisms that initiate PHP signaling remain enigmatic (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several genes necessary for PHP expression have been identified that function as presynaptic effectors in the motor neuron.
source: Several genes necessary for PHP expression have been identified that function as putative retrograde signals (Orr et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and presynaptic effectors in the motor neuron (Bruckner et al., 2017; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Dickman et al., 2012; Kiragasi et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012; Tsurudome et al., 2010; Younger et al., 2013), but the postsynaptic induction mechanisms that initiate PHP signaling remain enigmatic (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The postsynaptic induction mechanisms that initiate PHP signaling remain enigmatic.
source: Several genes necessary for PHP expression have been identified that function as putative retrograde signals (Orr et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014) and presynaptic effectors in the motor neuron (Bruckner et al., 2017; Dickman and Davis, 2009; Dickman et al., 2012; Kiragasi et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2012; Tsurudome et al., 2010; Younger et al., 2013), but the postsynaptic induction mechanisms that initiate PHP signaling remain enigmatic (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PHP induction and expression at a subset of synapses within a single motor neuron has never been demonstrated at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: Indeed, PHP induction and expression at a subset of synapses within a single motor neuron has never been demonstrated at the Drosophila NMJ.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: PHP is expressed exclusively at one of two motor neuron subtypes that innervate most muscles at the Drosophila NMJ, Type Is and Type Ib.
source: PHP is expressed exclusively at one of two motor neuron subtypes that innervate most muscles at the Drosophila NMJ, Type Is and Type Ib.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PHP expression patterns.

claim: Type Is motor inputs exhibit smaller boutons, less subsynaptic reticulum (SSR), higher basal release probability, and do not participate in PHP adaptation over chronic time scales.
source: Type Is motor inputs exhibit smaller boutons, less subsynaptic reticulum (SSR), higher basal release probability, and do not participate in PHP adaptation over chronic time scales (Lnenicka and Keshishian, 2000; Newman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Type Ib motor neurons have larger boutons, more elaborate SSR, and lower basal release probability.
source: In contrast, Type Ib motor neurons have larger boutons, more elaborate SSR, and lower basal release probability, which is enhanced after loss of postsynaptic GluRs (Newman et al., 2017), demonstrating that PHP is expressed exclusively at Type Ib synapses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Type Ib basal release probability is enhanced after loss of postsynaptic GluRs.
source: In contrast, Type Ib motor neurons have larger boutons, more elaborate SSR, and lower basal release probability, which is enhanced after loss of postsynaptic GluRs (Newman et al., 2017), demonstrating that PHP is expressed exclusively at Type Ib synapses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PHP is expressed exclusively at Type Ib synapses.
source: In contrast, Type Ib motor neurons have larger boutons, more elaborate SSR, and lower basal release probability, which is enhanced after loss of postsynaptic GluRs (Newman et al., 2017), demonstrating that PHP is expressed exclusively at Type Ib synapses.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A reduction in phosphorylated (active) levels of CaMKII occurs specifically in the postsynaptic density of Ib boutons.
source: Further, a reduction in phosphorylated (active) levels of CaMKII, presumably related to PHP inductive signaling, occurs specifically in the postsynaptic density of Ib boutons (Goel et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2017), suggesting a possible mechanism for the specificity of retrograde PHP signaling to the Ib motor neuron.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The reduction in pCaMKII at Ib boutons suggests a possible mechanism for the specificity of retrograde PHP signaling to the Ib motor neuron.
source: Further, a reduction in phosphorylated (active) levels of CaMKII, presumably related to PHP inductive signaling, occurs specifically in the postsynaptic density of Ib boutons (Goel et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2017), suggesting a possible mechanism for the specificity of retrograde PHP signaling to the Ib motor neuron.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research.

claim: GluRIIARNAi knock-down effectively phenocopies GluRIIA mutants.
source: Together, this demonstrates that postsynaptic knock down of the GluRIIA subunit effectively phenocopies GluRIIA mutants and induces the robust expression of PHP.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 showing similar GluRIIA levels, mEPSP amplitudes, and quantal content between GluRIIA mutants and G14>GluRIIARNAi.

claim: Postsynaptic knock down of the GluRIIA subunit induces the robust expression of PHP.
source: Together, this demonstrates that postsynaptic knock down of the GluRIIA subunit effectively phenocopies GluRIIA mutants and induces the robust expression of PHP.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 showing maintained EPSP amplitude despite reduced mEPSP amplitude.

claim: GluRIIA expression is almost completely absent in G14>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Similarly, GluRIIA expression is almost completely absent in G14 >GluRIIARNAi, with no significant difference in fluorescence intensity compared to GluRIIA mutants (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: There is no significant difference in GluRIIA fluorescence intensity between G14>GluRIIARNAi and GluRIIA mutants.
source: Similarly, GluRIIA expression is almost completely absent in G14 >GluRIIARNAi, with no significant difference in fluorescence intensity compared to GluRIIA mutants (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Quantitative PCR analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the level of transcripts encoding the GluRIIA subunit in G14>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Indeed, quantitative PCR analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the level of transcripts encoding the GluRIIA subunit in G14 >GluRIIARNAi, while levels of the other four subunits were not significantly changed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Levels of the other four GluR subunits were not significantly changed in G14>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Indeed, quantitative PCR analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the level of transcripts encoding the GluRIIA subunit in G14 >GluRIIARNAi, while levels of the other four subunits were not significantly changed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a small reduction in bouton number in both GluRIIA mutants and G14>GluRIIARNAi compared to controls.
source: In addition, we quantified synaptic growth in these genotypes, finding a small reduction in bouton number in both GluRIIA mutants and G14 >GluRIIARNAi compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as reported previously (Choi et al., 2014; Schmid et al., 2006; Sigrist et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior research.

claim: mEPSP amplitude is largely reduced in both GluRIIA mutants and G14>GluRIIARNAi compared to wild type and G14-Gal4/+.
source: Finally, we examined synaptic physiology, which revealed a large reduction in mEPSP amplitude in both GluRIIA mutants and G14 >GluRIIARNAi compared to wild type and G14-Gal4/+ (Figure 1D,E and Supplementary file 1), while EPSP amplitudes were not significantly changed between these genotypes because of a homeostatic enhancement in presynaptic glutamate release (quantal content; Figure 1D,H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: EPSP amplitudes were not significantly changed between GluRIIA mutants, G14>GluRIIARNAi, wild type, and G14-Gal4/+ because of a homeostatic enhancement in presynaptic glutamate release.
source: Finally, we examined synaptic physiology, which revealed a large reduction in mEPSP amplitude in both GluRIIA mutants and G14 >GluRIIARNAi compared to wild type and G14-Gal4/+ (Figure 1D,E and Supplementary file 1), while EPSP amplitudes were not significantly changed between these genotypes because of a homeostatic enhancement in presynaptic glutamate release (quantal content; Figure 1D,H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D,H.

claim: A single Ib and a single Is motor neuron bifurcates to innervate both muscle 6 and 7 at the muscle 6/7 NMJ.
source: At the muscle 6/7 NMJ, a single Ib and a single Is motor neuron bifurcates to innervate both muscle 6 and 7, with ~60% of the boutons from each motor neuron subtype innervating the larger muscle 6, and ~40% innervating the smaller muscle 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 60% of the boutons from each motor neuron subtype innervate the larger muscle 6, and approximately 40% innervate the smaller muscle 7.
source: At the muscle 6/7 NMJ, a single Ib and a single Is motor neuron bifurcates to innervate both muscle 6 and 7, with ~60% of the boutons from each motor neuron subtype innervating the larger muscle 6, and ~40% innervating the smaller muscle 7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: M6>Gal4 enables strong and biased expression of Gal4 on muscle six without impacting synaptic growth or function.
source: Thus, M6 > Gal4 enables strong and biased expression of Gal4 on muscle six without impacting synaptic growth or function.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no significant differences in muscle surface area, bouton number, BRP puncta, or synaptic physiology.

claim: GluRIIA expression is near-absent specifically on muscle 6 in M6>GluRIIARNAi, while GluRIIA expression on the adjacent muscle seven is unperturbed.
source: We observed a near-absence of the GluRIIA signal specifically on muscle 6, while GluRIIA expression on the adjacent muscle seven was unperturbed (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: There is a small but significant reduction in synaptic growth on muscle 6 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Quantification of synaptic growth on muscles 6 and 7 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi revealed no significant change on muscle 7, while a small but significant reduction was observed on muscle 6, as expected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by bouton number quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is no significant change in synaptic growth on muscle 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Quantification of synaptic growth on muscles 6 and 7 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi revealed no significant change on muscle 7, while a small but significant reduction was observed on muscle 6, as expected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by bouton number quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: M6>GluRIIARNAi effectively and specifically eliminates GluRIIA expression on muscle six without altering glutamate receptor expression on the adjacent muscle 7.
source: Thus, M6 > GluRIIARNAi effectively and specifically eliminates GluRIIA expression on muscle six without altering glutamate receptor expression on the adjacent muscle 7.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of GluRIIA and GluRIID fluorescence shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mEPSP amplitudes on muscle 6 were diminished at M6>GluRIIARNAi NMJs.
source: As expected, mEPSP amplitudes on muscle 6 were diminished at M6 > GluRIIARNAi NMJs, while mEPSP amplitudes were not affected on the adjacent muscle 7 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: mEPSP amplitudes were not affected on muscle 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: As expected, mEPSP amplitudes on muscle 6 were diminished at M6 > GluRIIARNAi NMJs, while mEPSP amplitudes were not affected on the adjacent muscle 7 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: EPSP amplitude was similar on both muscles 6 and 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi and not significantly different compared to wild type.
source: Results of electrophysiological recordings were consistent with this last model: EPSP amplitude was similar on both muscles 6 and 7 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi and not significantly different compared to wild type (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: Quantal content was selectively enhanced only at synapses innervating muscle 6 in M6>GluRIIARNAi, while quantal content at synapses innervating muscle seven was unaffected.
source: Indeed, quantal content was selectively enhanced only at synapses innervating muscle 6, while quantal content at synapses innervating muscle seven was unaffected (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B,E.

claim: PHP can be induced and expressed exclusively at a subset of synapses within the same motor neuron without influencing neurotransmitter release at neighboring sites.
source: Thus, PHP can be induced and expressed exclusively at a subset of synapses within the same motor neuron without influencing neurotransmitter release at neighboring sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiology data from M6>GluRIIARNAi showing compartmentalized PHP expression.

claim: PHP can be acutely induced and expressed through a pharmacological blockade of the postsynaptic GluRs using a 10-min incubation in the presence of philanthotoxin-433 (PhTx).
source: PHP can be acutely induced and expressed through a pharmacological blockade of the postsynaptic GluRs using a 10-min incubation in the presence of the antagonist philanthotoxin-433 (PhTx; [Frank et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PhTx application results in an acute reduction in mEPSP amplitude due to blockade of GluRIIA-containing receptors in the postsynaptic muscle, but EPSP amplitudes are maintained because of PHP expression.
source: This results in an acute reduction in mEPSP amplitude due to blockade of GluRIIA-containing receptors in the postsynaptic muscle, but EPSP amplitudes are maintained because of PHP expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of PhTx.

claim: PhTx application caused a large reduction in mEPSP amplitudes at wild-type muscles 6 and 7, as well as muscle 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: As expected, this caused a large reduction in mEPSP amplitudes at wild-type muscles 6 and 7, as well as muscle 7 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi, while a small reduction in mEPSP amplitude was observed at muscle 6 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: A small reduction in mEPSP amplitude was observed at muscle 6 of M6>GluRIIARNAi following PhTx application.
source: As expected, this caused a large reduction in mEPSP amplitudes at wild-type muscles 6 and 7, as well as muscle 7 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi, while a small reduction in mEPSP amplitude was observed at muscle 6 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: EPSP amplitudes at both muscles 6 and 7 in wild type and M6>GluRIIARNAi NMJs were maintained at similar levels following PhTx application due to the homeostatic enhancement of quantal content.
source: Interestingly, EPSP amplitudes at both muscles 6 and 7 in wild type and M6 > GluRIIARNAi NMJs were maintained at similar levels (Figure 4A,D) due to the homeostatic enhancement of quantal content (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,D,E.

claim: PHP can be acutely induced and chronically expressed at distinct presynaptic release sites within the same neuron according to the state of GluR functionality at postsynaptic compartments opposing these sites.
source: Together, this demonstrates that PHP can be acutely induced and chronically expressed at distinct presynaptic release sites within the same neuron according to the state of GluR functionality at postsynaptic compartments opposing these sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PhTx experiments showing PHP can be acutely induced at muscle 7 despite chronic PHP at muscle 6.

claim: The RRP is defined as the pool of vesicles that are primed and available for immediate release upon strong synaptic stimulation.
source: The RRP is defined as the pool of vesicles that are primed and available for immediate release upon strong synaptic stimulation (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Synaptic vesicles are highly mobile and can rapidly traffic between adjacent boutons at presynaptic terminals.
source: In particular, synaptic vesicles are highly mobile and can rapidly traffic between adjacent boutons at presynaptic terminals (Darcy et al., 2006; Kahms and Klingauf, 2018), and vesicle pools can span multiple presynaptic terminals (Staras et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vesicle pools can span multiple presynaptic terminals.
source: In particular, synaptic vesicles are highly mobile and can rapidly traffic between adjacent boutons at presynaptic terminals (Darcy et al., 2006; Kahms and Klingauf, 2018), and vesicle pools can span multiple presynaptic terminals (Staras et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There is a ~65% increase in the estimated RRP size that is restricted to boutons innervating muscle 6 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: We observed a ~ 65% increase in the estimated RRP size that was restricted to boutons innervating muscle 6 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi, similar in magnitude to what has been reported for muscle 6 synapses in which PHP is expressed following PhTx application (Müller et al., 2015) and by loss of GluRIIA (Kiragasi et al., 2017; Weyhersmüller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by RRP measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant change in RRP size was observed at synapses innervating the adjacent muscle 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: However, no significant change in RRP size was observed at synapses innervating the adjacent muscle 7 (Figure 5A,E).
evidence: This is supported by RRP measurements shown in Figure 5A,E.

claim: The homeostatic modulation of the RRP is restricted to presynaptic terminals that oppose postsynaptic compartments with reduced GluR functionality, and does not 'spread' to influence vesicle pools at adjacent release sites.
source: Thus, the homeostatic modulation of the RRP is restricted to presynaptic terminals that oppose postsynaptic compartments with reduced GluR functionality, and does not 'spread' to influence vesicle pools at adjacent release sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the compartmentalized RRP changes observed in Figure 5.

claim: There is no major difference in the anatomical number of active zones at NMJs of wild-type and GluRIIA mutants.
source: Although there is no major difference in the anatomical number of active zones at NMJs of wild-type and GluRIIA mutants (Frank et al., 2006; Goel et al., 2017; Penney et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2006), an increase in the fraction of active zones that participate in release has been reported following the expression of PHP (Davis and Müller, 2015; Newman et al., 2017; Penney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An increase in the fraction of active zones that participate in release has been reported following the expression of PHP.
source: Although there is no major difference in the anatomical number of active zones at NMJs of wild-type and GluRIIA mutants (Frank et al., 2006; Goel et al., 2017; Penney et al., 2012; Schmid et al., 2006), an increase in the fraction of active zones that participate in release has been reported following the expression of PHP (Davis and Müller, 2015; Newman et al., 2017; Penney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The value of N is significantly increased following PhTx application and in GluRIIA-mutant synapses.
source: Indeed, the value of N is significantly increased following PhTx application and in GluRIIA-mutant synapses (Müller et al., 2012; Weyhersmüller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The value of N increased in GluRIIA-mutant NMJs compared to wild type at both muscles 7 and 6.
source: Based on this result, the value of N increased in GluRIIA-mutant NMJs compared to wild type at both muscles 7 and 6 (Figure 6D,H), consistent with what was reported following acute PHP expression and indicating that chronic PHP expression requires the recruitment of additional functional release sites to participate in presynaptic neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6D,H.

claim: A similar increase in N was observed at muscle 6 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Further, a similar increase in N was observed at muscle 6 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi (Figure 6H), while no significant change was found at muscle 7 (Figure 6D), suggesting that the biased induction of PHP results in the compartmentalized expression of the same mechanisms observed in GluRIIA mutants (Figure 6A,E).
evidence: This is supported by variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: No significant change in N was found at muscle 7 in M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: Further, a similar increase in N was observed at muscle 6 in M6 > GluRIIARNAi (Figure 6H), while no significant change was found at muscle 7 (Figure 6D), suggesting that the biased induction of PHP results in the compartmentalized expression of the same mechanisms observed in GluRIIA mutants (Figure 6A,E).
evidence: This is supported by variance-mean analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Retrograde PHP expression is achieved by elevating the RRP and recruiting additional functional release sites to participate in transmission, with specificity according to the excitability state of their postsynaptic partners.
source: Therefore, retrograde PHP expression is achieved by elevating the RRP and recruiting additional functional release sites to participate in transmission, with specificity according to the excitability state of their postsynaptic partners.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the compartmentalized changes in RRP and N observed in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Reductions in postsynaptic CaMKII activity have been proposed to mediate the induction of retrograde PHP signaling.
source: However, reductions in postsynaptic CaMKII activity have been proposed to mediate the induction of retrograde PHP signaling (Haghighi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Modulations to postsynaptic CaMKII phosphorylation occur in a synapse-specific and activity-dependent manner at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: Indeed, modulations to postsynaptic CaMKII phosphorylation has been demonstrated to occur in a synapse-specific and activity-dependent manner at the Drosophila NMJ (Hodge et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Reductions in the level of phosphorylated (active) CaMKII were observed specifically at postsynaptic densities of Type Ib boutons following PhTx application and in GluRIIA mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea, reductions in the level of phosphorylated (active) CaMKII were observed specifically at postsynaptic densities of Type Ib boutons following PhTx application and in GluRIIA mutants (Goel et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the mean intensity of pCaMKII in Ib postsynaptic densities only on muscle 6 of M6>GluRIIARNAi.
source: We observed a significant reduction in the mean intensity of pCaMKII in Ib postsynaptic densities only on muscle 6 of M6 > GluRIIARNAi, while no significant difference was observed at Ib synapses in the adjacent muscle 7, nor were any changes found at Is synapses on either muscle (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7.

claim: No significant difference in pCaMKII was observed at Ib synapses in the adjacent muscle 7 of M6>GluRIIARNAi.
